title: Perpetua and Felicity
hook: a young noblewoman and an enslaved woman, both new mothers, face the arena together, and one reaches out a hand to lift the other

segments.voice: Yesterday, Justin's Sunday, and your line was on the day called sunday. Who did you send something to, the way the deacons carried bread to the absent? Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A father is on his knees in a prison in Carthage, in North Africa. He's begging his daughter. Have pity on my gray hair. Have pity on your mother, your brothers. Have pity on your baby son, who won't live without you. His daughter is Vibia Perpetua, well born, educated, a new mother, nursing her child in a cell. She has been arrested as a Christian. All she has to do is say she isn't one. The strange thing about this story is who tells it. For a long stretch of the account, the words are Perpetua's own: her prison diary, written in the first person, kept by the people who loved her.
screen: `ALL SHE HAS TO DO IS DENY IT.`

segments.voice: Perpetua answers her father with a water jug. She points to one lying nearby and asks him: can that be called by any other name than what it is? No, he says. So, she says, I can't call myself anything other than what I am, a Christian. In prison with her is Felicity, an enslaved woman, heavily pregnant. Felicity is afraid of a quiet kind of thing: that her pregnancy will hold back her execution, and she'll die later, without her friends, among common criminals. The others pray with her, and she goes into labor in the prison. She gives birth to a daughter, and a Christian woman takes the baby to raise as her own. So now there are two new mothers, one free and well born, one enslaved, with nothing in common by the rules of their city, and everything in common by the rules of their faith. On the day in the arena, the account says, the two women are thrown down by a wild cow. Perpetua gets up first. She sees Felicity on the ground, goes to her, gives her her hand, and lifts her up. And the two of them stand together. Before the end, the martyrs give one another the kiss of peace. Churches that remember them still name them together, side by side, the noblewoman and the slave. Some readers notice how much the account pays attention to small things: a jug, a father's gray hair, a woman pinning up her hair in the arena. It reads less like a legend about saints than a diary about people.
screen: `A WATER JUG: I AM WHAT I AM.`
`SHE GAVE HER HAND AND LIFTED HER UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone's hand. If there's someone beside you, a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, take their hand for this minute, without needing to explain. If you're alone, rest one hand in the other, and bring to mind someone whose hand you'd hold if you could, someone who's been knocked down lately. Picture going to them and lifting them up. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. If you don't, simply hold the picture of the two of you standing together. The bell holds the time.
Perpetua and Felicity. A noblewoman and an enslaved woman, both new mothers, remembered side by side. When one fell, the other gave her hand and lifted her up.
Your line: sisters. Today, offer a hand, literal or not, to someone the world sorts into a different place from you. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians who keep a calendar of saints remember Perpetua and Felicity together, on one day, and their story is sometimes read or preached then.

notes: The index says they died 'holding hands' (AD 203). The Passion (ch. 20) says Perpetua gave Felicity her hand and lifted her up and they stood together, then (ch. 21) the martyrs exchanged the kiss of peace. The script follows the text and states no date. Consider adjusting the index hook.

All quotations are paraphrased: the father's plea (ch. 5), the water jug (ch. 3), Felicity's fear and childbirth (ch. 15), the arena (ch. 20). Confirm details, including 'a wild cow' and Perpetua pinning up her hair.
Feast days are not stated in the script (Catholic and Anglican calendars keep March 7; both names are in the Roman Canon); confirm the howItsDone wording.
Original: 'Christiana sum' at the hearing before Hilarianus (ch. 6). Confirm wording against the Latin text.
Felicity is described as enslaved (conserva); the script avoids stating ages.

Editor pass: Felicity's fear now follows ch. 15 (dying later among common criminals, not 'strangers'); the water jug is no longer placed 'in the cell'; 'churches still say their names together' and 'often read' softened.
